senses.definition: (dated outside Mid-Atlantic US) The living room of a house, or a room for entertaining guests; a room for talking; a sitting-room or drawing room.

quotes.text: So, after a spell, he decided to make the best of it and shoved us into the front parlor. 'Twas a dismal sort of place, with hair wreaths, and wax fruit, and tin lambrekins, and land knows what all.
quotes.reference: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter XII, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y.; London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:

senses.definition: (archaic) The apartment in a monastery or nunnery where the residents are permitted to meet and converse with each other or with visitors from the outside.
(dated) A comfortable room in a public house.

quotes.text: Immediately at hand was a small, mean public-house - one of those dingy establishments that seem to express, by their morbid and retiring appearance, a certain anxiety to escape the eye of the police - and into the parlour of this hostel Quin promptly led the way.
quotes.reference: 1913, Norman Lindsay, A Curate in Bohemia, Sydney: N.S.W. Bookstall Co., published 1932, page 135:

quotes.text: There had been a surprise party and some had entered his hotel parlour to get drink; before he was aware of it the accordion was being played in the room.

senses.definition: (chiefly Southern US) A covered open-air patio.
A shop or other business selling goods or services specified by context.

senses.definition: A shed used for milking cattle; a milking parlor.
